conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that high-quality randomized trial evidence robustly demonstrates a large, statistically significant reduction in vertebral fractures for denosumab compared with placebo.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
The evidence contradicts the premise: denosumab does reduce vertebral fracture risk in postmenopausal osteoporosis.

The pivotal FREEDOM trial—an international, randomized, placebo-controlled, phase 3 study of 7,868 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis—found that denosumab significantly reduced new vertebral fractures compared with placebo. The cumulative incidence of new radiographic vertebral fracture was 2.3% with denosumab versus 7.2% with placebo (risk ratio 0.32; 95% CI 0.26–0.41; P<0.001), a roughly 68% relative risk reduction, with denosumab also reducing nonvertebral and hip fractures (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19671655/; https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0809493). This benefit was sustained through the trial's 7-year open-label extension, with 10-year data showing continued low fracture incidence and BMD gains (referenced via https://www.drugs.com/monograph/denosumab.html?references=1). The FDA-approved prescribing information likewise states Prolia "reduces the incidence of vertebral, nonvertebral, and hip fractures" in this population (https://prescriberpoint.com/therapies/prolia-49e5afe). Similar vertebral fracture reductions (~66%) were also seen in a Japanese trial cohort.

One retrieved source, a JABFM review, offers a dissenting note, concluding that despite BMD increases, "denosumab did not reduce fracture compared with bisphosphonates"—but this compares denosumab to another active treatment, not placebo, and doesn't negate the placebo-controlled FREEDOM findings (https://www.jabfm.org/content/jabfp/36/1/175.full.pdf).

**Conclusion:** The premise that denosumab does not reduce vertebral fracture risk is incorrect. High-quality randomized trial evidence (FREEDOM/NEJM) robustly demonstrates a large, statistically significant reduction in vertebral fractures versus placebo, sustained over a decade of follow-up. Any debate in the literature centers on comparative effectiveness versus other agents (e.g., bisphosphonates), not on whether denosumab works versus no treatment.
